title: Bike, Bus or Taxi in Lima?
paragraphs: Hi everyone! Last month I started using the new bike-share system in Lima, and now I love it. Today I want to compare it with the bus and with a taxi.

The bus is cheaper than a taxi, but it is slower in the morning. A taxi from my flat to the university costs 18 soles. The bus costs only 2 soles, but it takes forty minutes. With a bike, I need only twenty-five minutes, and a day pass costs 5 soles.

Of course, a bike is not perfect. When it rains, the road is more dangerous, and I don't have a place to put my bag. Also, there are not enough bike stations in some neighbourhoods. The station near my house is always empty at eight o'clock!
My advice: download the app and wear a helmet. Take the bike lanes when you can, because they are safer than the main roads. I feel healthier and more awake now. Are you going to try it this week?

title: The Missing Wallet
paragraphs: On Saturday morning, Daniela went to the market in Quito with her cousin. She bought tomatoes, bread and a small plant for her mother. Then she looked in her bag, and her heart stopped. Her wallet wasn't there.

'Think,' said her cousin. 'Where did you have it last?' Daniela remembered the bus. She ran to the bus stop, but the bus was gone. She felt terrible because the wallet had forty dollars, her student card and a photo of her grandmother.
A man at the stop saw her face. 'Are you looking for a brown wallet?' he asked. 'The driver found it under a seat and gave it to the office at the end of the line.'

Daniela and her cousin took another bus to the office. A woman gave them the wallet. Nothing was missing! Daniela wanted to thank the driver, so she wrote him a note and left a small gift. That night she told her mother, 'Next time, I'm going to keep my wallet in my front pocket.'

title: Greetings from Toronto
paragraphs: Hi Valentina,
How are you? I'm writing from Toronto, and I have so much to tell you! I arrived two weeks ago, and my host family is very kind. They have a big house near a lake, and I have my own room.

School is different here. Classes start at nine, and we change classrooms every hour. In my first week, I got lost three times. The teachers were patient, and a girl called Priya showed me the way. Now we eat lunch together every day.

The food is also new for me. Yesterday I tried poutine for the first time. It's a dish with chips, cheese and brown sauce. I didn't like it very much, but my host dad laughed and said, 'Everybody loves it after the third time.'
The weather is cold already, and I need a better coat. Next weekend we're going to a big market with my host family, and I'm going to buy a warm one.
Write soon and tell me about home!
Take care,
Joaquín

title: Pizzería Don Carlo
paragraphs: Pizzería Don Carlo, Buenos Aires – 4 stars out of 5
My friends and I went here last Friday after the football match. The restaurant is small, but the waiters are very friendly, and we didn't wait long for a table.

We ordered two large pizzas: one with cheese and tomato, and one with ham and onion. The cheese pizza was better than the other one. It was hot, and the bread was soft inside and crispy outside. The ham pizza was a bit too salty for me.
The prices are not high. Our two pizzas, three drinks and one dessert cost 14,500 pesos. There were four of us, so each person paid about 3,600 pesos.

The only problem is the noise. There were too many people, and the music was too loud. Next time, I'm going to go on a weekday, and I'm going to sit outside. I recommend this place to anyone who loves pizza.

title: Ximena and Her Cake Business
paragraphs: Ximena Torres is seventeen and lives in Puebla, Mexico. Two years ago, she started a small business and now she sells cakes online. We talked to her this week.
Interviewer: How did you start?
Ximena: I made a chocolate cake for my brother's birthday, and his friends loved it. They asked me for cakes for their families. After that, I opened a page on Instagram.
Interviewer: How much do you charge?
Ximena: A small cake costs 250 pesos, and a big one costs 450 pesos. I buy all the ingredients myself, so I don't earn very much yet.
Interviewer: Is it difficult to study and work?
Ximena: Sometimes. I bake on Saturdays and Sundays, and I do my homework at night. I usually go to bed late, but I'm happy.
Interviewer: What are your plans?
Ximena: In June I'm going to finish school. Then I'll study business at university, and one day I'm going to open a real shop.

title: My Phone-Free Weekend
paragraphs: Saturday, 8:00 a.m. Today is the first day of my phone-free weekend. My sister challenged me, and I said yes. I'm going to turn off my phone for forty-eight hours. I'm a little nervous.

Saturday, 1:00 p.m. This morning I was bored. I kept looking for my phone in my pocket. Then I took my bike to Parque Bicentenario in Santiago and read a book for two hours. I didn't take photos, so I looked at the trees instead.
Saturday, 9:00 p.m. My friend Camila came to my house because she couldn't reach me. We laughed a lot, and we made a plan for the cinema. It was strange to talk without sending messages.

Sunday, 6:00 p.m. I didn't touch my phone all weekend. I felt calm, and I slept better. When I turned it on, I had two hundred messages! Most of them were from a group chat about nothing important. Will I do it again? Yes, but maybe only on Saturdays.

title: Visit the City Museum of Bogotá
paragraphs: Welcome to the City Museum of Bogotá!
Discover five hundred years of history in one afternoon. Our museum is open from Tuesday to Sunday, from 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. We are closed on Mondays.
Tickets: Adults 12,000 pesos. Students with a card 6,000 pesos. Entry is free on the first Sunday of every month.

What can you see? On the ground floor, you can see old maps and photos of the city. On the first floor, there is an exhibition about music, from traditional songs to modern rock. Don't miss the roof terrace: from there, you can see the mountains.
Please remember: you can take photos, but don't use a flash. Don't touch the objects. Leave big bags in the lockers near the entrance.
Join a free guided tour at 11:00 or at 3:00. A tour takes about one hour. Our guides speak Spanish and English. For groups of ten or more people, please call us before you come.

title: Students in San José Reduce Plastic
paragraphs: A high school in San José, Costa Rica, started a recycling project in January, and the results were very good. In six months, the students reduced the plastic waste in the school by half.

The project was organised by fifteen students from the environmental club. First, they put coloured bins in every corridor. Then they asked the cafeteria to stop using plastic cups. Reusable cups were sold for 1,500 colones each, and more than three hundred were bought in the first month.
The plastic that was collected was taken to a recycling centre every Friday. With the money, the club bought plants for the school garden.
'At first, many students didn't care,' said Andrea Mora, the leader of the club. 'But we made short videos and put posters on the walls. Now everybody sorts the rubbish!'
The school is planning a new project for next year: a workshop to repair old bikes and phones.

title: How to Make Arepas at Home
paragraphs: Arepas are a popular food in Venezuela and Colombia. You can eat them for breakfast, lunch or dinner. This recipe makes six arepas, and it takes about thirty minutes.
You need: two cups of white corn flour, two and a half cups of warm water, a teaspoon of salt and a little oil. For the filling, you can use cheese, eggs or chicken.
Step 1: Pour the water into a large bowl and add the salt. Step 2: Add the flour slowly and mix with your hands. Wait for five minutes. The dough must be soft, but it must not stick to your fingers.

Step 3: Make six balls and press each one flat. Step 4: Heat a pan with a little oil. Cook each arepa for about seven minutes on each side. When you knock on it, it sounds hollow. Step 5: Cut each arepa open and add the filling.
Tip: Don't use too much water. If the dough is too wet, add a little more flour.

title: My First Job at a Café
paragraphs: Three weeks ago I got my first job. I work at a small café in Montevideo on Saturdays and Sundays, from ten to four. I'm seventeen, and I want to save money for a trip to Brazil next summer.

On my first day, I was very nervous. I dropped a tray with three coffees, and everyone looked at me. My boss, Señora Inés, only smiled and said, 'It happens to everybody.' She was so kind that I relaxed.

Now I know the menu, and I can make a good cappuccino. I also learned how to use the cash register. A coffee costs 120 pesos, and a sandwich costs 250 pesos, so I practise adding prices quickly in my head.

The job isn't easy. I stand all day, and my feet hurt at night. Some customers are rude, but most of them are nice and leave a tip. Last Sunday, a man left 100 pesos and said my coffee was the best in the street!
I earn 4,000 pesos for each day, and I'm saving half. I'm learning a lot about money, patience and teamwork.
